title: The AI opportunity for Europe
subtitle: Dinner remarks by Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at The International AI Summit
contents: SPEECH The AI opportunity for Europe Dinner remarks by Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at The International AI Summit Dublin, 13 October 2026 AI is a general purpose technology that can improve global living standards and the global knowledge frontier by expanding access to information and raising productivity. That said, delivering the benefits from AI depends on a host of different actors playing their part in supporting the transformation of the economy. The list is long and includes: the developers of AI frontier models (whether proprietary or open-weight); the builders of the various layers of the AI infrastructure stack; the entrepreneurs designing the customised AI products that can best unlock productivity gains in individual sectors or in relation to specialised tasks; the research and development community that can accelerate scientific discovery and compress the time lag between invention and commercial application; the operators of the energy systems that must respond to this new source of energy demand; the financial system that is required to appropriately value AI-related assets and finance AI production and AI adoption, while also incorporating AI into its own processes; the education and training sectors that must re-design instruction, learning and evaluation methods; and, finally, the managers and workers that must implement revised business processes at the sector and firm levels to maximise the benefits of AI. This transformation also poses many challenges for political systems, civic society, policymakers and regulators at national, European and global levels in relation to the ethical, fiscal, governance and legal issues posed by AI. How these political economy issues are resolved will have a major bearing on the AI transition path, including the appropriate speed of adjustment that balances the societal benefits, costs and risks posed by AI. Given the scale and breadth of the AI challenge, a wide range of possible timelines and outcomes can be envisaged, depending on the rate of progress along each individual dimension. The uncertainty surrounding the impact of AI – in both the short term and the long term – is compounded by the interdependencies and complementarities across these different dimensions. For instance, the rollout of rapid progress in AI capabilities can be held back by bottlenecks in some areas, slowing the overall pace of AI adoption. In particular, how firms and labour market institutions navigate the re-orientation of the workforce is a key issue, with some occupations facing the prospect of higher demand due to complementarities with AI and others facing lower demand due to the scope for substitution by AI.[1] The net impact on employment will also depend on the evolution of labour costs versus token prices. The European Central Bank is closely monitoring and analysing the impact of AI on the euro area economy for several reasons.[2] First, the medium-term and longer-term positive impact of AI on the level of potential output and the trend growth rate of the economy has the potential to raise the speed limit of the economy, with direct implications for the financial system and monetary policy. For Europe, the potential for AI to offset the economic impact of the projected trend decline in the working-age population is especially valuable. Second, more immediately, AI is already a primary factor driving current activity levels in the euro area. We see this in terms of a higher rate of business investment (firms are set to devote around 10 per cent of their total investment to AI this year), an expansion in digital services sectors and the high global demand for European components and capital goods that are part of the AI supply chain. In turn, this is supported by expansion in AI-related lending, which accounts for roughly one quarter of recent credit growth to firms. In our surveys, we are also tracking the rate at which firms and workers are adopting AI. In our Survey on the Access to Finance of Enterprises for the fourth quarter of 2025, most firms reported that they were using AI: 64 per cent of firms said they were using it either experimentally or moderately, while only 7 per cent of firms reported that their use was “significant”.[3] Our survey of households indicates that the proportion of workers using AI has doubled over the last two years, with 52 per cent now reporting that they use AI at work, compared with 26 per cent in 2024.[4] In the aggregate, workers are reporting significant time savings, but these are highly concentrated in specific sectors and specialised tasks such as coding. Taken together, these surveys suggest that AI adoption in Europe is already significant and growing rapidly, even if it is too early to detect any material impact on aggregate productivity. In relation to the labour market, we do not yet see a major change in aggregate employment trends but hiring plans are muted, which especially affects the prospects for new graduates. The potential for AI to replace some types of workers may also weaken the bargaining power of workers, moderating wage growth and reducing the labour share in total income. In our surveys, there is significant variation across industries, with workers in sectors benefiting from the AI infrastructure buildout currently more optimistic than those in knowledge-intensive sectors that face greater AI substitution risk. At the same time, it is also important to appreciate that the quantitative scale of the European AI surge is of a different order to the AI boom in the United States or East Asia. Over the last two years, digital investment in the United States has grown twice as fast as in the euro area, while US workers spend two to three times as much of the working week using AI as workers in the largest euro area economies.[5] In terms of the AI frontier, the Stanford AI Index calculates that the United States and China have produced 59 and 35 notable AI models, respectively, while France and the United Kingdom have produced one each. In terms of AI computing capacity, the United States hosts 75 per cent of the global aggregate, whereas Europe hosts just 5 per cent. Although international trade in AI goods and services can do much to spread the benefits of AI around the world, asymmetrical AI capacity across countries may generate a host of economic and geopolitical issues.[6] Third, it is likely that the global AI investment boom and expectations of a future global AI-driven productivity boost at longer-term horizons are plausibly contributing to the global increase in long-term interest rates.[7] Especially since the scale of the European AI boom is not of the same order as the global AI boom, the spillover to the euro area bond market means that the increase in long-term interest rates constitutes a material tightening of financial conditions for the euro area. This is a relevant factor for the ECB in determining the appropriate monetary policy stance. Fourth, the high equity valuations of AI firms and the global surge in AI-related debt issuance carry macroeconomic and financial stability risks in the event of even a temporary reversal in the expected rate of AI advancement or a decline in investor sentiment.[8] Accordingly, the financial stability and banking supervision functions of the ECB are closely monitoring the evolution of AI-related financial risks and, in addition, the associated cyber risks.[9] Fifth, the ECB has an extensive internal AI adoption agenda. Given that we are a knowledge-intensive organisation, AI has great potential to improve our analytical capacity and organisational efficiency. Over the last several years, I have been very impressed by the bottom-up initiatives of ECB staff to apply AI in a wide range of applications.[10] In closing, Europe has much to gain by seizing the AI opportunity. The ECB is committed to making sure that the AI transformation in Europe is underpinned by price stability and financial stability. In these remarks, I have highlighted that the aggregate impact of AI depends on a multi-dimensional transformation of the economy over an extended period. This is best achieved by recognising the collective interest shared by all sectors and policymakers in ensuring a sustainable AI transformation path. To this end, this AI summit provides an important opportunity to learn from each other and listen to a wide range of perspectives on AI. See, for example, Garicano, L., Li, J. and Wu, Y. (2026), Messy Jobs: The Work that AI Cannot Reach, Upriver Press. See also Lane, P.R. There is also upward pressure on the prices of AI-related components, such as semiconductors. The overall weight of such components in the consumer price index is relatively limited. At the global level, the large financing needs of AI frontier companies are largely being met through equity issuance and, increasingly, private credit. These risk-taking channels are highly sensitive to global risk appetite. See also: Lagarde, C. (2026), “Where AI risks meet”, welcome address at the tenth annual conference of the European Systemic Risk Board, Frankfurt am Main, 1 October; Anand, K., Kazinnik, S., Leonello, A., and Panetti, E. (2026), “Financial stability in the age of artificial intelligence: the role of algorithmic architecture”, Research Bulletin, No.143, ECB, 21 May; Cartea, Á., Colliard, J.E., Foucault, T., Hoffmann, P., Graumans, R. and Sigaux, J.D. (2026), “Artificial intelligence and financial markets”, Discussion Papers, No. 32, ECB, September. ECB Banking Supervision is also ensuring that the banking system is responding appropriately to the benefits and risks of AI, including cyber risk. See Elderson, F. (2026), “Strengthening operational resilience for the age of AI”, keynote speech at the Goldman Sachs European Financials Conference 2026, Zurich, 3 June. More broadly, AI is accelerating the digitalisation of the financial and payments systems. The ECB has taken a pro-active approach to financial digitalisation, including through its development of the digital euro and (via its Pontes and Appia projects) by facilitating the use of central bank money in settling transactions on digital financial platforms. On the regulatory challenges posed by the asymmetric understanding problem (whereby AI agents might understand humans better than humans can understand the behaviour of AI agents), see Brunnermeier, M.K. (2026), “Artificial Intelligence and the Brave New World in Finance”, paper prepared for the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium, Federal Reserve Bank of Kansas City, August. title: Ensuring resilience in the face of uncertainty
subtitle: Keynote speech by Frank Elderson, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB and Vice-Chair of the Supervisory Board of the ECB, at the ECB-Bank of England Conference on supervising climate risk in a non-linear world
contents: SPEECH Ensuring resilience in the face of uncertainty Keynote speech by Frank Elderson, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB and Vice-Chair of the Supervisory Board of the ECB, at the ECB-Bank of England Conference on supervising climate risk in a non-linear world Frankfurt am Main, 14 October 2026 It is a pleasure to open this joint ECB-Bank of England conference. Bringing together experts across disciplines from 18 countries and three continents to discuss how we can ensure resilience in an increasingly non-linear world, this event could hardly be more timely. For much of modern finance, risk management has rested on a simple but consequential assumption: with enough data, sufficient information about borrower behaviour, robust models and a solid understanding of historical patterns, banks can estimate the losses they may face with a reasonable degree of precision. These estimates inform how banks price risk, set aside provisions for expected losses and determine how much capital they need to absorb any large, unexpected losses. This approach works well when the underlying relationships are broadly stable and has long served as a useful basis for managing financial risks. And of course, today’s modelling is already supplemented by additional layers of risk management, including model overlays, stress testing, underwriting, risk appetite setting and other processes. But the world facing us today is becoming more complex, more interconnected and more uncertain almost by the day. Think about geopolitical fragmentation, demographic change, artificial intelligence and quantum computing and, of course, the central theme of this conference: the risks from the ongoing climate and nature (C&N) crises. These macro trends differ in many respects. They differ in origin. They differ in scope. They differ in speed. Yet they all share a common denominator: they arise in complex and highly interconnected systems, which often exhibit non-linear behaviour. This means that small changes can spread and trigger disproportionately large effects. These macro trends can amplify shocks through feedback loops. They can lead to abrupt transitions through tipping points. Events that were considered remote tail risks yesterday are moving closer to tomorrow’s baseline. Addressing non-linearities is undoubtedly challenging but still manageable as long as we remain in the realm of what is measurable. However, an even bigger challenge arises when we enter a world characterised by what Frank Knight termed uncertainty, as distinct from risk, or what John Kay and Mervyn King later popularised as radical uncertainty.[1] The underlying idea is the same: a form of uncertainty in which future events, their probabilities and even the relevant outcomes cannot be measured with any meaningful degree of confidence. Today I would like to use a simple framework to explore this challenge. The distinction between what we know, what we know we don’t know, and what we don’t even know we don’t know. Or put differently: known knowns, known unknowns and unknown unknowns. The world we know: the known knowns of C&N risks Let me begin with what we already know about C&N risks. Over the past decade, banks and supervisors have made substantial progress in identifying, quantifying and managing C&N risks.[2] Together, we have built the foundational architecture needed to capture the known knowns of C&N risks in risk management, stress testing and scenario analysis.[3] Today, we not only see and feel the effects of rising temperatures; increasingly, we can measure them. Thanks to better tools, better data and better modelling, we are increasingly able to quantify the direct damage caused to the economy by C&N risks.[4] Just think about the heavy toll this summers’ extreme weather took on economic activity, labour productivity[5] and supply chains.[6] Importantly, we also increasingly understand the transmission channels to the financial risk categories facing banks. For example, with better climate hazard and geo-location data, banks can better model the financial impacts of droughts and flooding on traditional financial risk metrics such as loss given default (LGD). We know banks’ initial estimate of the impact of different transition scenarios on their capital position. And we also know that since 2022 the average share of interest income earned from carbon-intensive sectors by significant supervised banks has remained consistently above 70%. We know the average energy performance of the properties they finance. We know what share of exposures they have in areas vulnerable to physical risk and what proportion of those exposures, in turn, has deteriorating credit quality. While many of these impacts still rely on estimates, banks have made significant strides in recent years, thanks also to the availability of public data sources, which cover an increasing number of physical risk hazards.[7] But as important as this progress is, it only tells part of the story.[8] We know that many of the C&N risks that matter most are, by their very nature, forward-looking. And we know that because these risks are very different from past events, they are not fully understood and remain difficult to quantify. The progress made so far therefore provides a springboard for a more difficult, but necessary conversation: a conversation about some of the fundamental challenges of these risks and uncertainty, a conversation not only about what we know, but also about what we know we do not yet know. What remains uncertain: the known unknowns of C&N risks And that brings me to the second category in our framework: the known unknowns. These are risks that we know exist, but whose timing, magnitude or probabilities remain uncertain. This is not a new challenge. Economic forecasting operates in a similar environment. The economy, like the climate, is a complex adaptive system. We cannot forecast it with precision, but we can explore plausible scenarios and assess our resilience against them. C&N risks provide several examples: We know that tipping points exist but we do not know exactly when they will be reached. Worryingly, scientists have identified several components of the Earth system for which the tipping point may already be approaching, including the dieback of the Amazon rainforest and the collapse of the Atlantic Meridional Overturning Circulation. We also know that compound events can amplify impact. We do not know precisely how such interactions will unfold. A severe drought will likely occur alongside a heatwave. Water scarcity could coincide with a major agricultural disruption. Physical damage could occur simultaneously with pressures on energy systems.[9] And we know that nature degradation can affect economic activity through complex and interconnected channels. We know that humanity is living well beyond most of its planetary boundaries.[10] In fact, seven of the nine planetary boundaries have already been transgressed. What remains uncertain is how these forces may interact, amplify each other and ultimately propagate through the economy and the financial system. In all these examples we run into a fundamental problem: the future impacts of climate change and nature degradation are, by definition, not reflected in the historical data used in traditional risk analysis. Using scenario analysis to address known unknowns When dealing with uncertainty, scenario analysis is an indispensable tool. Scenarios are best understood not as forecasts, but rather as structured explorations of plausible futures. Their purpose is not to tell us what will happen, but to help us think more systematically about what could happen. They allow us to identify vulnerabilities, test assumptions and investigate transmission channels that may otherwise remain hidden. Encouragingly, climate scenario analysis has advanced considerably in recent years. The Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) scenarios have become the global reference point for assessing how climate change may affect economies and financial systems over both short and long horizons. These scenarios have evolved to encompass a wider range of risks while also providing financial projections. By offering a publicly accessible set of scenarios, they have significantly improved the capacity of the central banking community to quantify climate risks in a consistent, transparent and comparable manner across jurisdictions. But scenarios are a starting point, not an endpoint. When facing uncertainty, we need to avoid a scenario “tunnel vision’’ where risk identification and capital planning becomes anchored to a narrow set of scenario narratives. With heightened uncertainty, the objective of scenarios should not only be to explore baseline pathways, but also to investigate how vulnerabilities might be exposed under extreme yet plausible conditions. And we know that the current climate scenarios have their limitations. As Simon Sharpe has observed, scientists are trained not to overstate risks, while risk managers are trained not to underestimate them. This distinction also matters for climate models designed by scientists. These models capture what can be quantified robustly, but not necessarily everything scientists know is likely to occur. Take thawing permafrost, for example. The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) concludes with high confidence that further warming will cause further thaw, thus releasing more carbon. Yet most global climate models do not represent this feedback directly. The separate adjustment used in the latest assessment still excludes abrupt thaw and interactions with Arctic wildfires. Research suggests that nature’s own emissions from thawing permafrost or wildfires could add as much as 0.6°C in an adverse scenario.[11] Similar limitations apply to additional emissions from warming wetlands and freshwater systems. Moreover, local transmission channels often differ substantially from global averages. The prudent conclusion is therefore to recognise that even the best available projections cannot yet fully capture every piece of relevant feedback, including some that are already well established. This is precisely why scenario analysis matters. Scenarios need to be tailored to local contexts, challenged and complemented with expert judgement. This is also why the NGFS encourages a more thoughtful and decision-relevant use of scenarios, rather than seeing climate scenarios as a box-ticking exercise.[12] Scenarios must be applied, not just adopted. They must be challenged, not just run. Many banks are still at a relatively early stage of integrating C&N risks into their core risk models. As a result, climate stress tests and scenario analysis are often used in the internal capital adequacy assessment process (ICAAP) primarily to calibrate buffers for risks that would otherwise not be covered. Yet these exercises only cover all the risk drivers that banks themselves deem material in around 15% of cases. At the same time, all the limitations and underestimations I have just mentioned also apply. It is therefore increasingly important that banks demonstrate a clear understanding of these limitations and that they take action early to build resilience and reduce their vulnerability to these growing risks over time. Scenarios must evolve, which requires a culture of continuous improvement, regular updates and close interaction between supervisors, practitioners and the research community. And that is precisely where this conference – which brings together experts across disciplines spanning the scientific and supervisory community – is invaluable because it can help to address some challenging questions. For example, how should supervisors and banks adapt scenario analysis in a world where uncertainty, non-linearity and tipping points cannot be fully captured by models? We look forward to hearing input you may have on the most effective ways to communicate model limitations, broaden the range of scenarios considered, and ensure climate risk assessments remain decision-relevant despite deep uncertainty. Or what role do expert judgement and tail-focused scenarios play in complementing quantitative analysis, and which risks require greater attention at the system level rather than at the institution level? And how can C&N risk analysis be translated into bank risk management, strategic decision-making and supervisory actions where banks underestimate risks? Radical uncertainty: building resilience for the unknown unknowns of the climate and nature crises Scenarios are well suited to exploring known unknowns, but they are less able to address radical uncertainty. This brings me to the third category: genuine unknown unknowns. The challenge with unknown unknowns is not only that we struggle to estimate probabilities or magnitudes, but that we do not yet know all the relevant states of the world and possible outcomes. We don’t even know what all the complex interactions between climate systems, ecosystems, societies and financial markets will be, so there’s no way we can actually measure them. We don’t yet know about all the complex feedback loops that only become visible once a shock unfolds. And we do not yet know about all the transmission channels that only emerge once critical thresholds have been crossed. But worryingly, there is growing evidence that the climate and nature crises are unfolding faster and more severely than expected, which may indicate that some of the complex interactions I mentioned might be coming our way sooner than we thought: Consider that the Arctic is warming at almost four times and Europe at roughly twice the global average,[13] while the most intense rainfall events are in some cases increasing faster than conventional climate models have captured. The Earth is also accumulating heat at a rate that recent observations suggest is higher than many model simulations anticipated.[14] In September the United Nations warned that El Niño is colliding with an already exceptionally warm planet, creating what it described as “being supersized before our eyes”.[15] Ocean heat has reached record levels, and the pace of ocean warming over the past two decades has been markedly faster than in earlier periods, suggesting that the earth's capacity to absorb excess heat may be changing in ways that we don’t fully understand.[16] Similarly, ecosystems are losing resilience, in some cases faster than earlier assessments anticipated.[17] Coral reefs, forests and wetlands are under growing pressure, weakening nature’s capacity to absorb shocks and increasing the risk of cascading impacts across ecological and economic systems. Until recently, many of these developments were poorly understood. Others may become visible only as shocks unfold and previously hidden interactions emerge. Their complex interactions cannot be fully anticipated, let alone incorporated into scenarios that capture every interaction across the climate, ecosystems, economies and financial markets. This brings us back to Simon Sharpe’s distinction. Scientific rigour requires caution in describing what cannot yet be demonstrated. Risk management requires similar caution in assuming that what cannot yet be modelled can be safely ignored. This is the realm of radical uncertainty rather than measurable risk. And repeated surprises on the upside should make us cautious about assuming that what remains unknown will be benign. The answer to unknown unknowns is therefore not just scenarios or risk modelling, but to build resilience against surprises. Resilience is not something we build after a disaster. Instead, it is something we invest in before shocks occur. Building resilience obviously includes maintaining sufficient capital, liquidity, operational capacity and strategic flexibility to absorb shocks that cannot be predicted in advance. But it is also about having a well-developed and risk-sensitive reaction function. This includes actively reflecting on what further role other layers of risk management, including underwriting, model overrides, risk appetite setting, portfolio steering and pricing could play. It also includes reflecting on the range of risk mitigants, such as insurance protection and governments’ more limited fiscal space to act as insurers of last resort. It also includes reflecting on climate adaptation and mitigation investment, and on how these investments can be deployed effectively to address longer-term risks. It also includes banks testing their reaction function regularly through scenarios and analysis of business model resilience to ensure their governance and decision-making structures are capable of responding swiftly when the risk landscape changes. This is at the heart of prudential transition planning.[18] Lessons for other macro trends subject to uncertainty And this brings me to my final point. Climate and nature-related risks are perhaps the clearest manifestation of non-linear dynamics and heightened uncertainty. But they are far from being the only one. The insights from addressing these challenges in climate risk are also relevant for other macro trends and risk drivers affecting banks, such as technological innovation, demographic change and geopolitical risks, to name just a few. As European banking supervision highlighted in its 2026-28 supervisory priorities, heightened uncertainty is a cross-cutting challenge spanning several risk areas, making the likelihood of extreme tail risks unprecedently high. Similarly to C&N risks, tackling these trends will require interdisciplinary cooperation well beyond prudential authorities. Take demography as a structural risk driver.[19] Now that supervisors have learned to analyse the drivers of C&N risk, they can build on the progress to interpret demographic trajectories as a structural risk driver affecting banks’ business models and risk profiles. Take rapid advances in artificial intelligence that have increased cyber and operational resilience risks. We know that these developments are already altering the cyber risk landscape, but we do not yet know the exact magnitude with which they will unfold. This is a classic known unknown for which backward-looking information alone is not useful. Yet this does not prevent supervisors from taking action.[20] Or take quantum computing as an example of a technology with non-linear effects. Quantum risk to cryptography is already a risk given that sensitive, encrypted information can be collected today and stored with the expectation that future technological advances may allow it to be decrypted in a “harvest now, decrypt later” fashion, leading to non-linear consequences. All these macro trends have a common denominator: uncertainty. There is uncertainty about the timing, impact, transmission channels and consequently the data and modelling challenges.[21] All of these macro trends could also have an impact on the sustainability of banks’ business models. They therefore all need an upscaled risk management framework, with scenario capabilities as a core pillar to help banks stay resilient and competitive over time. Conclusion Let me conclude. For much of modern finance, risk management has focused on understanding and measuring risks. That remains indispensable. But in an increasingly complex and interconnected world, building resilience requires more than that. If risk management is like driving along a winding mountain road, preparedness is not just about being able to react when a cliff suddenly appears. It is about having guardrails and contingency measures in place for when the road may veer dangerously close to the edge. For known knowns, our task is to measure. For known unknowns, our task is to prepare. And for unknown unknowns, our task is to build resilience. When reality repeatedly surprises us on the upside, prudence requires us to be careful about assuming that the risks we have not yet identified will somehow be benign. This conference, which brings together experts across disciplines, is an opportunity to deepen our understanding on all three fronts: on where we can sharpen our focus on what we can already identify and quantify, on where we need to further illuminate uncertainties that warrant further exploration, and on where we can strengthen resilience to weather radical uncertainty. Thank you for your attention and I look forward to the fruitful discussion. Kay, J. and King, M. (2020), Radical Uncertainty: Decision-making for an Unknowable Future, The Bridge Street Press. For more details on banks’ better preparedness to identify, quantify and manage C&N risks, see Elderson, F. (2025), “Banks have made good progress in managing climate and nature risks – and must continue”, The Supervision Blog, ECB, 11 July; and Elderson, F. (2025), “From charting the course to staying the course: the path ahead for climate and nature risk supervision”, keynote speech at the ECB industry dialogue on “Climate and nature risk management: taking stock and looking ahead”, Frankfurt am Main, 1 October. For more information about the increasingly sophisticated methods and tools developed by banks and shared by ECB Banking Supervision with banks across Europe, please see Elderson, F. (2026), “Good practices for advancing climate and nature-related risk management”, The Supervision Blog, ECB, 8 May; ECB (2026), Good practices for climate and nature risk management. Observations from the ECB’s five-year climate and nature risk programme (2020-25) , May; and ECB (2026), ECB report on good practices for climate and nature-related risk stress testing , May. This year’s droughts are already imposing significant economic costs across Europe. Initial estimates point to losses of at least €50 billion in the short term alone. The insurance firm Allianz estimates cumulative GDP losses of up to 7% between 2026 and 2030 in major European economies, equivalent to around USD 240 billion for France, USD 147 billion for Italy, USD 131 billion for Germany and USD 120 billion for Spain. For further details, see Allianz (2026), Too hot to grow. The economic costs of extreme heat , 28 May. According to United Nations estimates, workers' productivity declines by around 2% to 3% for every additional degree of heat above certain thresholds. Estimates suggest that the June heatwave alone may have resulted in €6.3 billion in productivity losses in Germany. For further details, see the World Health Organization’s web page on workplace heat stress. The exceptionally low water levels of the Rhine this summer, the lowest since records began in 1880, have not only disrupted transport and industrial production. They could also reduce Germany's economic recovery by up to 0.2 percentage points of GDP in the third quarter. In Romania, Hungary and France, low river levels have even disrupted electricity generation, affecting both nuclear and hydropower production. See Network for Greening the Financial System (2025), Leveraging physical climate risk data , September. Despite the notable strides made by banks under ECB supervision in integrating C&N risks into their risk management procedures, more still needs to be done to ensure they apply sound practices across all material portfolios, exposures and risk categories. For example, some banks may focus only on transition risks but not on physical risks – and vice versa – in certain portfolios. Some prudential transmission channels, such as operational or market risk, receive far less attention compared with credit risk. Furthermore, not all banks have included all material risk drivers, relevant portfolios or transmission channels in their C&N risk management. For more details on the lack of comprehensive coverage see Elderson, F. (2025), “Banks have made good progress in managing climate and nature risks – and must continue”, The Supervision Blog, ECB, 11 July The experience of a major German car manufacturer is a case in point. Back in 2024 flooding damaged an upstream aluminium supplier in Switzerland, disrupting production further down the supply chain. The flood itself was a known physical hazard. The broader consequence – namely, disruptions cascading through interconnected production networks – was much harder to model. For further details, see Arnold, M. and Dempsey, H (2024), “Porsche warns on profits as flooding hits aluminium supplier”, Financial Times, 23 July. See the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research’s web page on Planetary Boundaries – defining a safe operating space for humanity. Dinneen, J. (2026), “A Missing Piece in Climate Models: Nature’s Own Emissions”, Yale Environment 360, 18 June. NGFS (2026), Guide to climate scenario analysis for central banks and supervisors – 2025 version, 24 September. Rantanen, M., Karpechko, A.Y., Lipponen, A. et al. (2022), ”The Arctic has warmed nearly four times faster than the globe since 1979”, Communications Earth and Environment, 11 August; and World Meteorological Organization (2025), European State of the Climate – Report 2024 , 15 April. Hodnebrog, Ø., Myhre, G., Jouan, C., et al. (2024). “Recent reductions in aerosol emissions have increased Earth’s energy imbalance”, Communications Earth and Environment, 3 April. https://wmo.int/news/media-centre/el-nino-set-become-very-strong-raising-risks-of-extreme-weather-2027 World Meteorological Organization (2025), State of the Global Climate 2024 , 19 March. Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (2022), “Climate Change 2022: Impacts, Adaptation and Vulnerability”, Working Group II contribution to the IPCC Sixth Assessment Report, 28 February. For more information about prudential transition planning as a key tool for managing risk along a range of possible pathways but also for capitalising on business opportunities, see Elderson, F. (2026), “Good practices for advancing climate and nature-related risk management”, The Supervision Blog, ECB, 8 May. Montagner, P. (2025), “Europe’s demographic shift: what could it mean for banking supervision?”, The Supervision Blog, ECB, 25 November. Buch, C. (2026), “Addressing AI-enabled cybersecurity threats”, letter to the CEO of the significant institution, European Banking Supervision, Frankfurt am Main, 7 July; and Financial Stability Board (2026), “FSB Chair warns of risks arising from frontier Artificial Intelligence (AI) models”, press release, 31 August. See also Angeloni, I. and Claessens, S. (2026), “An EU Prudential Framework for Slow-Burning Risk Drivers”, European Parliament, September, for more about slow-burning risk drivers (SBRDs), which are factors that build up risks incrementally over time, adversely affecting the viability of banks beyond normal supervisory timelines.

title: IMFC Statement
subtitle: Statement by Christine Lagarde, President of the ECB, at the fifty-fourth meeting of the International Monetary and Financial Committee
contents: SPEECH IMFC Statement Statement by Christine Lagarde, President of the ECB, at the fifty-fourth meeting of the International Monetary and Financial Committee IMF Annual Meetings, 17 October 2026 Introduction The global economy has proven surprisingly resilient in the face of high uncertainty. The conflict in the Middle East continues to expose energy markets to sharp swings. Trade tensions and protectionist measures are weighing on confidence and contributing to a reconfiguration of trade flows. The global economy has held up thanks in part to the rise of artificial intelligence, with investment in technology supporting activity and trade, particularly in economies integrated into technology value chains. Risks nonetheless remain tilted to the downside for growth and to the upside for inflation. A return to an international economic order grounded in openness, predictability and the rule of law would help trade and investment flourish. Economic activity Despite global headwinds and the ongoing energy shock, the euro area economy has so far proved resilient. Growth was broad-based across most euro area countries and sectors in the first half of 2026. The September ECB staff projections foresee growth of 0.9% in 2026, 1.4% in 2027 and 1.5% in 2028. As the energy shock fades over the medium term, the projections see domestic demand benefitting from a recovery in real income over the medium term, driven by lower energy inflation and a resilient labour market. Rising government spending on infrastructure and defence, complemented by investment in AI and digital technologies, should also support growth. Export growth should pick up on the back of strengthening foreign demand, also driven by AI. The medium-term outlook is surrounded by uncertainty over how intense and long-lasting the Middle East conflict will be, and how the resulting shocks might propagate through the economy. Risks to growth are assessed to be on the downside. Fiscal sustainability remains a crucial anchor for broader economic stability. It is important to maintain sound fiscal policies, including by adhering to fiscal rules, and, where debt is high, to consolidate, re-prioritise spending and enhance the efficiency and effectiveness of public finances to rebuild buffers. Governments should strive to ensure that any fiscal response to the energy shock is temporary, targeted and tailored. In addition, policies that strengthen resilience to climate change can improve the economy’s ability to absorb climate-related shocks. These efforts should be complemented by structural policies that promote labour market participation, equip the workforce with the skills needed in an AI-driven economy and facilitate the diffusion of new technologies. Priorities include advancing the savings and investments union, improving access to risk capital and creating better conditions for innovative firms to scale up across the Single Market. Inflation Headline inflation increased to 3.8% in September, mostly reflecting a surge in energy inflation, and, to a lesser extent, an increase in food and services inflation. Core inflation increased slightly to 2.5%. The range of underlying inflation measures remained broadly stable in September and wages have so far shown no material response to the energy shock. Looking ahead, higher energy prices are expected to keep headline inflation well above target into the first half of 2027 and to gradually feed through to core and food inflation. Headline inflation is expected to decline after the first quarter as energy inflation falls, returning to around target towards the end of 2027. The risks to the inflation outlook are to the upside due, in particular, to the Middle East conflict and Russia’s unjustified war against Ukraine. A more intense or persistent energy shock could strengthen indirect and second-round effects, resulting in higher and more persistent inflation. Extreme weather could push up food prices. By contrast, a sustainable resolution of geopolitical conflicts, weaker energy pass-through or more risk-averse financial markets could lower inflation. Monetary policy The Governing Council decided to raise the key ECB interest rates by 25 basis points in September, following an increase of the same size in June. Our interest rate decisions are based on our reaction function, which comprises three criteria: our assessment of the inflation outlook and the risks surrounding it, in light of the incoming economic and financial data, the dynamics of underlying inflation; and the strength of monetary policy transmission. The inflation outlook points to higher inflation ahead, especially in the short term, given the latest developments in energy markets. However, we see no evidence at this stage of significant pass-through of energy prices to other prices and wages, beyond what we have already included in our projections. And while growth has been resilient, financing conditions have tightened, with long-term interest rates rising notably since our last meeting. This will slow growth and reduce pass-through by more than projected in our September exercise. Taking these three criteria together, the energy shock is too large to “look through” but a measured response remains appropriate to keep inflation in check. In setting future policy, we will make a comprehensive assessment of the incoming data based on our reaction function. In July, the Governing Council decided on the operational features and the onboarding process for the enhanced EUREP, the Eurosystem repo facility for central banks that was announced earlier this year. The new facility supports the smooth transmission of monetary policy and reinforces the international role of the euro. More than 30 central banks have expressed interest in EUREP in the past six months. Financial stability Sources of risk and vulnerabilities for euro area financial stability remain high. Continued geopolitical tensions, fiscal challenges and uncertainties around accelerated AI adoption continue to be causes for concern. The widespread concentration of critical third-party service providers introduces single points of failure for both financial and non-financial institutions. New frontier AI models have increased cyber risks and operational vulnerabilities. Euro area banks maintain strong capital and liquidity buffers and robust profitability, together with healthy and stable asset quality. These solid fundamentals should help navigate ongoing geopolitical uncertainties and effectively support lending to the economy. Strengthened prudential regulation and supervision since the global financial crisis has helped leave euro area banks in a strong position to withstand the unfolding economic challenges. Shocks could expose vulnerabilities among non-bank financial intermediaries, notably from concentrated AI-related exposures, amplifying market stress and creating spillovers across financial sectors. Banks’ exposures to non-banks and vulnerable firms could expose funding and credit vulnerabilities. Stress in private credit markets has continued, with private credit funds reporting outflows and reactivating redemption gates. Private market “semi-liquid funds” that allow for redemptions are becoming more prevalent, which could lead to greater liquidity mismatches in the future, but euro area financial institutions have limited direct exposure to private credit. This means, for now, that private credit in isolation is unlikely to be a source of financial instability in the euro area. Payment systems Central bank money must evolve to fulfil the needs of an increasingly digital economy. The Eurosystem is at the forefront of this evolution, bringing the stability and trust of central bank money to digital retail payments and tokenised finance in Europe. In the retail space we are preparing to complement cash with its digital equivalent – the digital euro – for day-to-day payments. The digital euro will further stimulate innovation and competition in retail payments, ensuring that the continued co-existence of public and private solutions underpins Europe’s strategic autonomy in payments. To lay the groundwork for a seamless and secure launch, we will run a 12-month internal pilot in the second half of 2027. Adopting the Regulation on the establishment of the digital euro by the end of 2026 is key to making this possible. In the wholesale space, the Eurosystem is developing new capabilities to ensure that central bank money can settle transactions in the growing market of tokenised assets. Pontes – the Eurosystem’s distributed ledger technology (DLT) solution that went live on 21 September – marks the first step in implementing our strategy to enable the development of a European tokenised ecosystem. This vision will be advanced under the Appia initiative, which aims to deliver a blueprint for this ecosystem based on common standards, shared network infrastructure and European governance. International cooperation We value the work of our global institutions and fora, particularly those that promote global macroeconomic and financial stability. We welcome the recent completion of the three major IMF reviews (Comprehensive Surveillance Review, Financial Sector Assessment Program Review and Review of Program Design and Conditionality), which strengthen the role of the IMF at the centre of the global financial safety net. Climate-related work should remain fully anchored in IMF operations, particularly surveillance. Multilateral efforts to help tackle global imbalances support coordination of domestic action that is required to minimise the risks from disorderly adjustment. The IMF’s analytical work on global imbalances and its improvements to the methodology for assessing external balances provide a strong basis for these efforts.

title: From climate and nature risks to economic resilience and competitiveness
subtitle: Keynote speech by Frank Elderson, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB and Vice-Chair of the Supervisory Board of the ECB, at the Green Swan 2026 Conference
contents: SPEECH From climate and nature risks to economic resilience and competitiveness Keynote speech by Frank Elderson, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB and Vice-Chair of the Supervisory Board of the ECB, at the Green Swan 2026 Conference Manila, 19 October 2026 Introduction We are living in a time of profound economic, geopolitical and technological uncertainty. Yet amid all this uncertainty, one thing is clear: climate change and nature degradation will continue to shape our economies and societies, and we will have to deal with the consequences. Climate change and nature degradation are a certainty in an uncertain world. The events of this summer have reminded us of that reality in the most tangible way possible. For Europe, the summer of 2026 was not simply another warm season. It was the warmest summer ever recorded in Western Europe, marked by severe droughts, devastating wildfires, water scarcity and mounting pressure on ecosystems across the continent.[1] Water levels in major European rivers fell to exceptionally low levels, affecting transport, industry and energy production. At the same time, large areas of land were destroyed by fires and important economic sectors faced disruptions.[2] Europe is warming faster than any other continent at more than twice the global average.[3] The human toll has been severe, with tens of thousands of excess deaths linked to extreme heat recorded during the summer months.[4] This summer also served as a reminder of how much our economies depend on nature. Water scarcity affected not only households and agriculture, but also manufacturing, transport and energy production. Across Europe, pressure on ecosystems highlighted the fact that healthy forests, soils, rivers, wetlands and oceans are not just environmental assets, but that they provide essential ecosystem services on which economic activity relies every day, and which often go unnoticed until they are put under strain.[5] Taken together, this summer’s events conveyed a simple but powerful message: climate and nature are not external to our economies. They are embedded within them and, increasingly, they are becoming a macroeconomic concern. This raises a number of important questions. How can we strengthen economic resilience in a world of more frequent climate and nature-related shocks? How do we ensure that, as we pursue the green transition, we also strengthen competitiveness, energy security and long-term prosperity? And which barriers still stand in the way of the investment needed to make that happen? Let me address each of these questions in turn. Climate and nature crises pose a systemic risk Let me take one step back. When a drought, flood or wildfire occurs, attention immediately and naturally focuses on the event itself. Taken in isolation, the economic and financial consequences may appear manageable. Yet individual events only tell part of the story. It is a bit like focusing on individual symptoms while ignoring the underlying disease. The more important question is how climate and nature-related shocks add up, interact, reinforce one another and affect economies over time. In this context, I am reminded of an observation by the economist and author Simon Sharpe.[6] Scientists are trained not to overstate risks. Risk managers are trained not to underestimate them. This points to a trade-off that central bankers and supervisors know well. Faced with uncertainty, we can err in both directions: we can reassure ourselves too readily that a risk will not materialise, or we can raise a false alarm. Reducing the likelihood of one increases the likelihood of the other. Our task is therefore to reduce uncertainty as far as possible through better data and analysis, carefully assess the consequences of getting it wrong, and respond proportionately.[7] We cannot predict the future with certainty, but we can try to understand how risks may evolve, identify vulnerabilities and strengthen resilience. This is the perspective central banks and supervisors should take when looking at climate and nature crises. The challenge is compounded by the fact that we are not dealing with a static risk. As temperatures rise and physical hazards intensify, the economic consequences are becoming increasingly dynamic and material. A growing body of evidence shows that climate-related shocks can leave lasting economic scars. Extreme heat reduces labour productivity. Droughts affect agriculture, industry and transport. Floods damage infrastructure and disrupt production. Investment may be postponed, populations may relocate and economic output can remain below trend for years after major events.[8] They do not just affect economic activity, but already increasingly affect prices as well. This summer provided fresh examples of this: high temperatures and low water levels disrupted parts of Europe’s energy system and contributed to higher wholesale electricity prices, while extreme weather continues to influence food prices.[9] Climate shocks therefore affect not only growth but also inflation dynamics. These risks are also inherently cross-border. Food price shocks, supply chain disruptions and migration pressures do not stop at national frontiers. Nature-related risks operate through similar channels. Recent ECB research suggests that severe water scarcity alone could put up to 24% of the euro area’s economic output at risk. At the same time, a significant share of economic activity and bank lending remains exposed to flood risk.[10] The lesson is not that a single drought, flood or wildfire will trigger a macroeconomic crisis. As these disasters become more frequent and severe, the lesson is that a hotter planet and nature degradation are increasingly becoming structural drivers of economic and financial outcomes. This matters directly for central banks and supervisors. Our job description is clear. We are responsible for maintaining price stability and safeguarding banks’ safety, soundness and financial stability. As climate and nature risks increasingly affect productivity, growth, inflation and the resilience of the financial system, taking them into account falls squarely within our mandate. That is why central banks need macroeconomic models and forecasting procedures that reflect the impact of climate change and nature degradation and keep track of the changing structure of the economy.[11] That is also why forums such as the Green Swan Conference matter. Bringing together central bankers, supervisors, policymakers and academics from around the world is itself an important contribution to resilience. In a world that is facing increasing geopolitical fragmentation and risks, international cooperation and collective efforts remain some of our most essential and valuable tools for advancing our knowledge and addressing shared risks. Economic resilience requires both adaptation and mitigation This brings me to my second point. When discussing the impact of the climate and nature crises, it is important to distinguish clearly between adaptation and mitigation. Adaptation addresses the consequences. Mitigation addresses the causes. We need both. The reality is that the consequences of climate change and nature degradation will continue to unfold for years to come. Past emissions have already warmed the planet and set in motion changes that cannot simply be reversed overnight. Meanwhile, greenhouse gases continue to accumulate in the atmosphere. We cannot make the risks we already face disappear.[12] That means societies, households, firms and financial institutions need to take pre-emptive action and strengthen their resilience. We need advanced early-warning systems and infrastructure that can withstand extreme weather. We need better water management, including, flood prevention, energy-efficient cooling and measures against water leakage. We need more resilient energy systems and cities, transport networks and production systems that can continue functioning under more challenging climatic conditions. Adaptation is not optional, it is a necessity for our economies to remain resilient and competitive in the future. This is not starting from zero. Across Europe, regions and cities are already investing in climate resilience, while initiatives at EU level are supporting adaptation and strengthening our preparedness for water scarcity, floods and wildfires.[13] [14] These efforts show what can be done. The challenge now is to accelerate them and bring them to scale. But adaptation alone is not enough. Without mitigation, the scale of adaptation required becomes progressively larger and more costly. In some places, particularly low-lying coastal areas and small island states, climate change may eventually make adaptation extraordinarily difficult, if not impossible. Mitigation therefore remains essential. The more effectively we can mitigate climate change and protect nature, the lower the future adaptation costs will be. And the better we adapt, the more resilient our economies will become during the transition. There is no silver bullet. But there is a clear direction of travel. The transition is a competitiveness strategy Let me now turn to what I believe is one of the most important debates currently taking place in Europe: the green transition as a central pillar of competitiveness. It is perhaps also an area where policymakers and businesses in many parts of Asia are already providing valuable lessons. And the next panel in today’s conference, on resilience building in the real economy, with business sector representatives from the Philippines, Japan and Europe, couldn’t be timelier in this respect. In Europe, resilience, energy security, competitiveness and the green transition are still too often perceived as competing objectives. I believe that is the wrong way to think about it. Firms cannot remain competitive if their operations become increasingly vulnerable to climate and nature-related shocks. Instead, resilience and energy security are increasingly becoming preconditions for competitiveness. And if managed well, the transition, which includes both adaptation and mitigation, can reinforce all three. The question is no longer whether the global economy will transition to green energy. The question is who will be well positioned as we move forward along the transition path. And when the transition is complete, who will own and finance the assets of the new economy, and who will be left holding the stranded assets? The good news is that many elements of the transition increasingly make economic sense on their own merits. Consider energy. Europe remains heavily dependent on imported energy, much of it fossil fuel-based.[15] This dependency creates vulnerabilities, exposes households and firms to geopolitical shocks and amplifies uncertainty. Recent events have once again demonstrated the economic costs of these dependencies. By contrast, renewable energy and electrification can strengthen resilience by reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels and improving energy security. Yet Europe is still far from an electrified economy. Electricity currently accounts for only around a quarter of final energy consumption.[16] This leaves considerable potential for electrification across transport, buildings and industry to reduce fossil fuel dependence while supporting both decarbonisation and economic resilience.[17] The good news is that the economics of the transition have fundamentally improved. Renewable energy technologies are increasingly cost-competitive and, in many cases, already cheaper than new fossil-fuel alternatives.[18] The International Energy Agency estimates that a significant share of residential heating, road transport and industrial heat could already be electrified cost-effectively.[19] And we are now beginning to see the resilience benefits of cleaner electricity systems. During recent energy shocks, electricity prices have proved less vulnerable to fossil-fuel price fluctuations in countries with greater low-carbon generation. Spain is a case in point: as solar generation has expanded, its electricity prices have become less dependent on gas markets and less volatile.[20] The same logic applies beyond energy. Healthy soils, reliable water resources and resilient ecosystems are not just environmental assets. They are also productive assets. Agriculture, food production and many industrial activities depend on them. Preserving natural capital and adapting to a changing climate therefore helps safeguard food security, strengthen resilience and support long-term competitiveness. The case for the green transition is therefore no longer solely an environmental one. It is also very much a competitiveness, resilience and security argument. By reducing dependence on imported fossil fuels, a more electrified, renewables-based energy system strengthens strategic autonomy, makes the economy better able to absorb shocks and reduces exposure to energy price volatility, which may also, through indirect and second-round effects, affect headline inflation over time.[21] A successful transition is not merely about avoiding future costs. It is also about capturing opportunities. This makes the case for clean energy a macroeconomic argument. That is why I continue to believe that what Europe needs – what the world needs – is not simply a transition and adaptation strategy. What we need is a “smart transition”: one that puts sustainable and resilient competitiveness at its core, combines mitigation and adaptation, and invests in technologies, infrastructure, skills and institutions that strengthen prosperity while reducing risk. What is holding investment back? If the economic rationale is increasingly clear, an obvious question follows: why is progress not faster? Research consistently points to two barriers in particular. The first is uncertainty, understood in a broad sense to include political, economic and regulatory uncertainty. The second is access to finance.[22] Let me start with uncertainty. Economic theory is clear. Households, firms and financial institutions only commit capital to long-term investments when they believe the rules of the game will remain broadly stable. This is especially true for transition-related investments such as energy infrastructure, industrial transformation and electrification. All these investments require large upfront commitments and long planning horizons. Policy instability increases the cost of waiting and when investors wait, progress slows. Evidence from the euro area bank lending survey confirms that uncertainty weighs on demand for loans to finance green investment.[23] Yet uncertainty affects more than investment decisions. It also affects financing conditions. As uncertainty rises, banks become more cautious, tighten credit standards and reduce their willingness to take risk.[24] The result is a double constraint: firms postpone investment and financing becomes harder to obtain, which in turn can further amplify the impact on demand. This is particularly damaging for green investment, which requires substantial initial investments and long-range planning. Let me be clear. This is not a case for rigid policymaking. Instead, I am making a case for predictability. The transition requires certainty for long-term planning. The second challenge is financing. The scale of the challenge should not be underestimated. Around the world, meeting climate and nature objectives will require unprecedented levels of investment. In Europe alone, this amounts to hundreds of billions of euros in additional investment every year for years to come.[25] Many transition-related investments are capital-intensive and have long payback periods. That makes them sensitive to financing conditions. Banks have an important role to play, particularly in Europe’s bank-based financial system.[26] At the same time, deeper capital markets will be necessary to complement bank financing and help innovative firms and technologies to scale up. The scale of investment required also underlines the importance of international capital flows and cross-border cooperation. International cooperation also helps safeguard fairness by ensuring that firms investing in the transition are not placed at a systematic disadvantage relative to those that do not. This requires a level playing field, underpinned by common standards, credible international commitments and mutual trust. Credibility also means not backtracking on legislative commitments on which firms have based long-term investment decisions. Without such predictability, progress will inevitably become both more difficult and more costly.[27] Conclusion Let me conclude. Earlier, I described climate change and nature degradation as a certainty in an uncertain world. The summer of 2026 demonstrated precisely why. Climate and nature risks are no longer distant possibilities. They are already shaping economic outcomes today. The conclusion is clear. Building stronger resilience will require a proactive and comprehensive response that combines adaptation and mitigation with sustained investment, effective international cooperation and, above all, the resolve to act before risks fully materialise. When properly executed, investing in adaption and the transition is not merely about avoiding damage. It is an opportunity to build a more productive, more resilient and more competitive economy. A world of greater resilience is also a world of greater prosperity. The task now is to ensure that we move towards that future deliberately, credibly and with sufficient speed. Climate change and nature degradation may be a certainty in an uncertain world, but how we respond to them remains very much a matter of choice. Thank you for your attention. title: Euro liquidity lines and the international monetary system
subtitle: Remarks by Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the CF40-Euro50 luncheon “Monetary System Beyond the Dollar”
contents: SPEECH Euro liquidity lines and the international monetary system Remarks by Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the CF40-Euro50 luncheon “Monetary System Beyond the Dollar” Shanghai, 21 October 2026 The provision of liquidity is a basic task for a central bank.[1] The ECB injects liquidity through its refinancing operations (currently the main refinancing operations and the longer-term refinancing operations, with very long-term refinancing operations and targeted longer-term refinancing operations deployed in the past) and asset portfolios (previously built up under the asset purchase programme and the pandemic emergency purchase programme).[2] Since the ECB only has domestic counterparties in its refinancing operations, it is essential to complement the domestic liquidity framework with international liquidity lines. These lines, which consist of both repo and swap lines, mitigate adverse spillovers in the event of increased demand for euro liquidity abroad and/or impairment in cross-border euro liquidity flows. In the absence of international liquidity provision, such shocks might exert upward pressure on euro money market rates or disrupt the functioning of securities markets and the banking system, and thereby impair monetary policy transmission. In recent years, the world economy has undergone profound structural shifts related to geopolitics and changes in the international financial system. These shifts have altered the dynamics of global trade and financial integration and suggest that the macroeconomic and financial environment will remain uncertain and potentially more volatile. More frequent financial disruptions and possible knock-on effects on euro area financial markets have the potential to hamper the smooth transmission of monetary policy. Given their backstop pricing, international liquidity lines are designed to be drawn down only in response to shocks and in crisis situations. However, their mere existence – even without being drawn upon – can help to prevent adverse market dynamics from arising in the first place. Empirical evidence suggests that the ECB’s liquidity lines have been effective in reducing financial pressures on euro funding markets.[3] This year, the ECB decided to enhance the Eurosystem repo facility for central banks (EUREP) to make it more flexible and effective in supporting the smooth transmission of euro area monetary policy.[4] Under EUREP, the Eurosystem provides backstop euro liquidity to non-euro area central banks against high-quality euro-denominated collateral, with appropriate risk mitigants. The updated framework introduces standing access, in principle, for all central banks, unless excluded on the grounds of, in particular, money laundering, terrorist financing or international sanctions. The framework will enable central banks in jurisdictions outside the euro area to swiftly address risks of euro liquidity shortages. These changes aim to make the facility more flexible, broader in terms of its geographical reach, and more relevant for global holders of euro securities. Central banks onboarded to EUREP will receive euro liquidity in the form of loans against high-quality euro-denominated collateral, priced at the main refinancing operations (MRO) rate plus a spread set by the Governing Council to preserve the backstop character of the facility. The maturity of a single transaction will range from one day to one week and may be extended. The maximum line size per individual central bank is €50 billion. Onboarded central banks can use EUREP funds flexibly, without ex ante restrictions. After completing the onboarding process, central banks will be able to draw from the facility as of the fourth quarter of 2026. Appropriate risk mitigants are in place to adequately protect the Eurosystem. More than thirty central banks have expressed interest in EUREP in the past six months and the onboarding of first foreign central banks to the enhanced facility was completed at the beginning of October. EUREP can be expected to exert a strong positive impact on the euro-denominated bond market, boosting the savings and investments union initiative. In particular, EUREP encourages the holding of euro-denominated debt securities by foreign central banks, which are price-insensitive investors. It also encourages the holdings of longer-duration bonds, since it enhances the liquidity of these bonds: the liquidity enhancement is considerable as EUREP offers same day liquidity of up to €50 billion off-market in a single transaction. Since reserve managers would be able to hold bonds from all euro area countries rather than just the most liquid bonds, EUREP also enhances the playing field between more liquid and less liquid euro area sovereign bonds, contributing to better integration of the euro area bond market. Importantly, this argument extends to Eurosystem-recognised supranational bonds (e.g. European Commission bonds) which suffer from lower liquidity than large sovereigns. Swap lines complement EUREP from a monetary policy perspective, strengthening the overall international liquidity lines framework. EUREP lends against euro-denominated collateral, which enables breadth of access. However, the collateral constraint limits its role: a country may have extensive euro liabilities and excessive self-insurance (by matching euro liabilities with euro assets) would be an undesirable equilibrium, whereas the availability of swap lines can facilitate more efficient liquidity risk management. Swap lines can be deployed against local-currency collateral, such that combined swap and EUREP access offers stronger overall support than EUREP alone. In particular, swaps are not contingent on having euro-denominated collateral. Thus, swaps have stronger signalling effects than EUREP alone in terms of access to liquidity, which helps to reduce the likelihood of escalating crises abroad and limits adverse spillovers to the euro area. In particular, provided fundamentals are sufficiently strong, the existence of swap lines can reduce the risk of adverse confidence shocks abroad becoming self-fulfilling. There are some differences in the transmission channels of swap and repo lines, which enhances their complementarity. In particular, swap lines work more directly through the bank credit channel, as recipient foreign central banks lend euro cash to their domestic banks, which then lend to the financial system. This is consistent with the theoretical literature showing that central-bank lending programmes reduce ex-post financing risk and encourage ex-ante investment through global banks operating across integrated financial markets. In this way, swap lines can provide deep, targeted euro liquidity support to the domestic banking system of selected partners, even if the lines are expected to be used only in times of crisis, while EUREP is mainly focused on supporting the functioning of euro-denominated debt securities markets at the global level. This is consistent with the empirical evidence that access to swap lines is associated with stronger cross-border bank credit flows, while repo-type access is closely tied to developments in securities holdings.[5] Since swap lines entail greater risks than EUREP, it is appropriate to provide them only to foreign central banks that are clearly capable of repaying their euro debt in due course, requiring the backing of a highly-rated sovereign. Careful calibration and assessment are also needed to mitigate potential overreliance and moral hazard.[6] From a European perspective, it is also sensible to restrict swap lines to jurisdictions where the impact on the euro area from defaults on euro-denominated debt or fire-sales of assets – including via indirect or network effects operating through the global financial system – have the potential to impair monetary policy transmission. Global trade, financial and supply chain linkages mean that seemingly isolated idiosyncratic shocks in one country or region – especially if the economy is large, a major financial centre or closely tied to the euro area – may transmit rapidly and unpredictably, escalate through network effects and pose a threat to monetary policy transmission. The monetary policy case for liquidity lines is reinforced by their dynamic interaction with other policy areas. In particular, liquidity lines can boost the international role of the euro, which further supports the ability of the ECB to achieve its monetary policy objectives.[7] Liquidity lines bolster confidence in the currency and reduce the associated risks, supporting its wider usage in trade invoicing and settlements. Liquidity lines also support expanded issuance of euro-denominated debt. Such an expansion can entail two dimensions: (i) an increase in the volume of (new) euro-denominated credit as a swap line would encourage foreign counterparts to borrow in euro, either through loans or market-based debt instruments; and (ii) currency switching, whereby some FX loans previously extended by European lenders (including through their global subsidiaries) in foreign currency might – if a currency backstop exists – be made in euro. Both of these channels strengthen the effectiveness of ECB monetary policy transmission.[8] Greater use of the euro internationally, in turn, supports the ability of the ECB to achieve price stability by increasing the international impact of euro area monetary policy and thereby influencing foreign demand as well as domestic demand. For example, a tightening of euro area monetary policy makes it more expensive for foreign entities to source euro denominated funding, which weighs on demand in economies that use the euro, particularly for debt issuance, as well as for trade invoicing and funding of working capital. This spillover of euro area monetary policy spills back via weaker foreign demand, reinforcing the monetary policy tightening. Furthermore, a stronger international role for the euro reduces the sensitivity of euro area import prices to external shocks by fostering invoicing in euro. The views expressed in these remarks are mine and should not be interpreted as representing the collective view of the ECB Governing Council. In addition, assets are purchased by the ECB and the national central banks for non-monetary policy portfolios under the agreement on net financial assets. See Albrizio, S., Kataryniuk, I., Molina, L. and Schäfer, J. (2021), “ECB Euro Liquidity Lines”, International Journal of Central Banking, Vol. 22, No. 4.; and Beck, R., Ferrari, M. and Titzck, S.
