title: Taking action for nature – investing in economic resilience and prosperity
subtitle: Keynote speech by Frank Elderson, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB and Vice-Chair of the Supervisory Board of the ECB, at COP17 Finance and Biodiversity Day
contents: SPEECH Taking action for nature – investing in economic resilience and prosperity Keynote speech by Frank Elderson, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB and Vice-Chair of the Supervisory Board of the ECB, at COP17 Finance and Biodiversity Day Yerewan, 26 October 2026 It is a pleasure to open the Finance and Biodiversity Day at COP17. The theme of this COP is “Taking Action for Nature’’. We have talked about the need for action for long enough. Now we need to act. Four years ago, the international community adopted the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, setting out a pathway to living in harmony with nature by 2050. The destination is set. The path is clear. But progress has remained limited. And nature has not stood still. It has continued to deteriorate. So we need to accelerate. Tangible progress requires a shift from targets to implementation, from awareness to engagement, from ambition to investment. COP17 must help us accelerate the journey. And finance has a central role to play. That should not come as a surprise: without investment, there can be no transition. But we need to get the economics right. Protecting and restoring nature is not simply spending. It is investment: investment in the natural capital on which our economies depend, investment in resilience, and investment in our future prosperity. That is why Finance and Biodiversity Day matters. When ecosystems falter, the economy is at risk Let me start with a fundamental question: why is nature so important to the economy? We tend to think of roads, bridges and electricity grids as critical assets that serve as the foundation of a modern economy. But there is another kind of infrastructure that we often take for granted: natural capital. Nature provides services without which large parts of our economies could not function. Water keeps our factories and farms running, healthy soils sustain our food systems, forests and wetlands regulate droughts and floods, oceans absorb heat and carbon. The World Bank estimates that as much as half of the world’s GDP relies on biodiversity, natural capital and ecosystem services.[1] Our own analysis shows that 72% of companies in the euro area depend on at least one ecosystem service. And 75% of euro area corporate lending goes to companies that are highly dependent on at least one ecosystem service.[2] The message is clear: nature is not peripheral to economic activity. It is fundamental to it. But even as we speak, the foundations of our economies are being depleted at an alarming rate.[3] When ecosystems deteriorate, firms face higher costs, lower productivity and supply chain disruptions. For far too long, we have treated nature as though it were free and inexhaustible. It is neither. We have mistaken the depletion of natural capital for economic prosperity. We counted the production. We counted the income. But we rarely – if ever – counted the soils depleted, the water systems stressed, the forests weakened or the ecosystems lost in producing it. In economic terms, we have been consuming our capital and calling it income. Nature is already presenting us with the bill. Depleted natural capital is already disrupting production, damaging supply chains and increasing costs. The consequences are already spreading from ecosystems to firms, from firms to balance sheets and from balance sheets into the financial system. This is not a future tragedy on the horizon. It is an economic reality unfolding around us. That is why taking action for nature is not only an environmental imperative. It is an economic and financial necessity because our future prosperity directly depends on it. The natural currency underwriting economic activity: water Water is perhaps the clearest example of what happens when we fail to account for natural capital. For too long, we have allowed our economies to function as though reliable supplies of clean water were an unlimited production input. But an economy cannot negotiate with an empty river, a depleted aquifer or a failed ecosystem. When we withdraw water faster than it can be replenished, we are not creating prosperity. We are fooling ourselves and failing future generations by consuming the capital on which future prosperity depends. Think about this summer’s heat-exacerbated drought conditions throughout Europe: major rivers, like the Rhine, Loire, Po and Danube, reached exceptionally low levels, forcing, among other things, the shutdown of critical nuclear power plants, while also negatively affecting hydropower and disrupting supply chains.[4] Drought also contributed to the severity of wildfires. These are not glimpses of a distant risk. They are stark signs of ecosystems already being pushed beyond their limits, with consequences that are already being felt by people and the economy. Unfortunately, our analysis suggests that the potential consequences could be much larger. Research involving the ECB, the London School of Economics and Oxford University has found that a 1-in-100-year drought event could put up to 24% of euro area economic output at risk.[5] Clearly, too little water is only half of the story. Too much water can be equally problematic. Nearly 12% of economic output in the euro area faces risks from insufficient flood protection.[6] The recent catastrophic events in Nepal and Bangkok are a stark reminder of the devastating human consequences alongside the destruction of infrastructure and economic assets. And there is a third dimension to consider: polluted water. Take PFAS, for instance. Known as “forever chemicals”, these pollutants are in a wide range of everyday products from textiles and cookware to batteries and food packaging. As the name suggests, they last an extraordinarily long time – and when they leach into the environment, they can be extremely damaging for people’s health and for entire ecosystems, all of which also comes at substantial economic cost. The European Commission estimates that, if current levels of PFAS pollution in Europe continue until 2050, the cost to society could reach €440 billion over that period. Treating polluted water alone could cost more than €1 trillion.[7] The economic challenge comes from water in all its dimensions: too little, too much, too hot, too dirty. And the effects differ across regions and sectors: agriculture here, manufacturing there and energy production somewhere else. When sufficiently widespread or persistent, the impacts can ultimately affect growth and inflation. Nature: our first line of defence against the climate crisis But the example of water also reveals something else: climate and nature cannot be separated. Healthy ecosystems act as our first line of defence against global heating and related extreme weather events. Europe is the fastest-warming continent. Temperatures have been rising by approximately 0.56 degrees Celsius per decade since the mid-1990s, more than double the global average. This summer again brought record temperatures, following on from 2025 which was the third-warmest year on record, and 2024, the warmest ever – so far. The interplay between temperature, the water cycle and soil quality illustrates why the climate and nature crises should be treated as a nexus. And perhaps nowhere is this more evident than in the ocean. The ocean is one of our planet’s greatest shock absorbers. It has absorbed around 90% of the excess heat from global warming and around 30% of global carbon dioxide emissions.[8] That is an extraordinary capacity. But extraordinary does not mean unlimited. Even the strongest buffer has its limits. And those limits are no longer theoretical; we are already breaching them. Seven of the nine planetary boundaries have already been transgressed. We are moving increasingly outside the safe operating space on which our economies and societies depend.[9] In other words, we are consuming the buffers that protect us from economic disruption and climate shocks at precisely the moment when those shocks are intensifying. Nature – an investment in economic resilience and prosperity Recognising nature as economic infrastructure has another important implication. If degrading nature can weaken our economies, preserving and restoring it can strengthen them. This matters particularly today, when maintaining prosperity, resilience and economic security has taken centre stage in the policy debate. Protecting nature is often framed as if it comes at the expense of competitiveness. However, that frames the problem backwards. As we seek to strengthen prosperity and economic security, nature should be seen as part of the solution rather than as part of a separate, often neglected, environmental agenda. Economic security depends on ecological security. Secure water supplies, resilient food systems, functioning ecosystems and reliable energy systems are strategic assets that reduce vulnerability to future disruptions. We should therefore stop treating investment in nature as a competing claim on prosperity and economic resilience.[10] It is investment in the productive capacity that makes lasting prosperity possible. There can simply be no lasting prosperity on a collapsing natural foundation. We cannot impoverish nature and expect our economies to flourish. Therefore, preserving and restoring nature is not simply an expenditure. It is an investment. We can invest in preserving and restoring natural capital now. Or we can pay increasingly through disrupted production, adaptation, reconstruction and lost economic capacity later. Nature will impose the adjustment regardless. The question is whether we manage that adjustment, or allow it to be imposed on us. From awareness to action So what does this mean for central banks and banking supervisors? Nature-related risks are global and systemic. They do not stop at borders, and no single jurisdiction can address them alone, which makes international cooperation more indispensable than ever. The current geopolitical fragmentation puts global cooperation at great risk. Encouragingly, the Network for Greening the Financial System (NGFS) shows that international cooperation is alive and can deliver. Bringing together 152 central banks and supervisors across more than 95 countries, alongside 24 observers, the NGFS has over time produced several reports that have helped us to develop common methodologies on risk assessment frameworks, supervision and legal risks.[11] A recently released compendium of good practices[12] covers 35 examples of how members assess the physical and transition risk impact of nature-related risks, together with six detailed case studies. In other words, the work of the NGFS has helped lay the groundwork for many of the central banks and supervisors now taking action to account for nature-related risks in their core activities. But the NGFS cannot do this alone. Nature-related financial risks need to remain firmly on the international financial agenda, including at the Basel Committee, the Financial Stability Board and the IMF. At the ECB, this shift from awareness to action is already well advanced. Because nature degradation can affect price stability, financial stability and the safety and soundness of banks, nature-related risks are increasingly part of the bread and butter of our work. In banking supervision, we expect banks to identify and manage not only material climate risks, but also nature-related risks, as part of ensuring banks remain safe and sound.[13] And our recently updated compendium of good practices shows that banks are increasingly doing just that, with around one-third of the practices relating specifically to nature.[14] Take price stability, for example. We have found that increases in food prices following extreme heatwaves and droughts are an upside risk to price stability.[15] Nature risks have therefore featured explicitly in our monetary policy assessment and communication in recent quarters.[16] Nature is not becoming a feature of central banking because central banks are becoming environmental policymakers. Quite the contrary: we are – and will remain – climate and nature policy takers. Nature is becoming a feature of central banking because the consequences of its degradation are affecting our mandate. Conclusion Let me conclude. Four years have passed since Kunming-Montreal. Nature has not waited. We have developed frameworks, methodologies and tools. But while our understanding improved, the underlying ecological crisis has continued to deepen. Today, 75% of land ecosystems and 66% of ocean ecosystems have been damaged, degraded or modified. Humanity is consuming natural resources around 1.7 times faster than ecosystems can regenerate them. The challenge is no longer simply getting to the destination. It is getting there fast enough before the road towards it disappears. Doing so will require investment at unprecedented scale. Protecting and restoring the natural infrastructure on which economic activity depends will require mobilising substantially greater private capital flows towards nature-positive investments, alongside public finance.[17] But the longer we delay restoring natural capital, the more costly and difficult restoration becomes. And that brings me back to the purpose of today’s event. I would like to leave you with three key questions that I hope will reverberate throughout this Finance and Biodiversity Day. First, how can we mobilise public and private finance at the scale needed to turn the Kunming-Montreal goals into reality? Second, how can governments, financial institutions, international organisations and other stakeholders work together to help turn nature-positive opportunities that are not yet bankable into investments that can attract capital? And third, how can policy, investment and partnerships help to mobilise finance for projects that generate public goods without direct revenue flows? Kunming-Montreal set the destination. COP17 must now accelerate the journey. Turning awareness into action. Turning targets into tangible results.Turning ambition into investment. Because nature is not waiting. Neither can finance. World Bank (2025), Mainstreaming Nature into World Bank Macroeconomic Models: Overview Report , Washington, D.C. Boldrini, S. et al. (2023), “Living in a world of disappearing nature: physical risk and the implications for financial stability”, Occasional Paper Series, No 333, ECB. Recently, the Deutsche Bundesbank published a study that shows the German banking sector is particularly highly dependent on ecosystem services linked to water. 75% of land surface ecosystems and 66% of ocean ecosystems have been damaged, degraded or modified. Around 80% of arable land worldwide is affected by soil erosion, salinisation and biodiversity loss. These pressures are projected to reduce global food productivity by 12% by 2040, increasing food prices by up to 30%. We are running an ecological deficit by using natural resources 1.7 times faster than ecosystems can regenerate them. A landmark report by the Intergovernmental Science-Policy Platform, published this year and approved by more than 150 member governments, warns that biodiversity loss is among the most serious threats to businesses. The exceptionally low water levels of the Rhine this summer, the lowest since records began in 1880, have not only disrupted transport and industrial production. They could also reduce Germany's economic recovery by up to 0.2 percentage points of GDP in the third quarter. For example, UNEP estimates that every dollar invested in integrated climate change and air pollution action generates around $15 in economic benefits. Today, more than 90% of the banks supervised by the ECB consider themselves to be materially exposed to climate and nature risks, and all have put in place the foundational frameworks needed to identify, assess and manage these risks. While banks have made substantial progress on climate risk, nature-related risks remain considerably less mature. For example, two-thirds of banks do not systematically link their materiality assessment on nature-related risks to a risk management response, and only a few have defined nature-related key risk indicators. Where such indicators exist, they are often used solely for monitoring, with no limits or thresholds to trigger management action Elderson, F. That means investment must increase by more than 2.5 times.

title: Next-day securities settlement, tokenisation and the transformation of Europe’s financial infrastructure
subtitle: Keynote address by Piero Cipollone, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at an EU T+1 Industry Committee event on “One year to T+1”
contents: SPEECH Next-day securities settlement, tokenisation and the transformation of Europe’s financial infrastructure Keynote address by Piero Cipollone, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at an EU T+1 Industry Committee event on “One year to T+1” Frankfurt am Main, 29 October 2026 We are approaching an important milestone.[1] Less than a year from now, on 11 October 2027, Europe will move to T+1 settlement. This means that the time from the moment a security is traded to the moment the buyer receives it and the seller is paid will be reduced from two days to one. This may sound like a technical change, but it is in fact much more significant. The transition to T+1 is part of a broader transformation of Europe’s financial infrastructure. And the objective is clear: to make Europe’s financial and payment system more efficient, more resilient and safer, and ultimately to make European financial markets more competitive. In the Eurosystem, we are contributing to this transformation across the full spectrum of our mandate. We are ensuring that banknotes remain available and fit for purpose. We are preparing for a digital euro. We are modernising wholesale payments and securities settlement. And we are working to enhance cross-border payments and harness new technologies such as distributed ledger technology (DLT).[2] These are not separate projects. They are different parts of the same strategy: ensuring that the euro and Europe’s financial markets are fit for the future in a rapidly changing world. From T+2 to T+1: an essential element of a broader modernisation effort The move to T+1 contributes to this broader strategy. It is about more than just reducing the time between trade and settlement to one day. A shorter settlement cycle can reduce market and counterparty risk. But, perhaps even more importantly for Europe, the transition is also forcing us to review our post-trade processes. It requires greater standardisation, automation and innovation. Inefficiencies that could be accommodated in a T+2 environment will become much more difficult to sustain under T+1. In that sense, T+1 is a catalyst for modernising European post-trade markets. And this is important for Europe’s competitiveness. Efficient post-trade infrastructure makes it easier for capital to flow across borders. It helps investors access European markets. And it supports the EU’s wider ambition to create deeper and more integrated capital markets. It also ensures that Europe keeps pace internationally with other major markets as they shorten their own settlement cycles. That is why the ECB, together with the European Securities and Markets Authority and the European Commission, strongly supports the market’s preparations for T+1. There is another lesson for Europe here which I believe is particularly important: we can deliver when we work together. Europe’s financial landscape remains complex and fragmented. Yet the work coordinated by the EU T+1 Industry Committee has shown that those differences do not need to stand in the way of common solutions. I would therefore like to congratulate everyone involved for the progress made so far. It is a powerful reminder of what Europe can achieve when public authorities and the private sector come together around a common objective. But we have not yet crossed the finish line. The coming months will be critical. Implementation and testing need to advance with the same determination and cooperation that have been the driving force behind the project so far. The Eurosystem is also responsible for operating TARGET2-Securities (T2S), our platform for securities settlement in central bank money through which cash and securities can be exchanged simultaneously across Europe.[3] And the key message here is a simple one: T2S already supports shorter settlement cycles. It already settles substantial volumes of transactions on a T+1 and even a T+0 basis. So we are not starting from scratch. At the same time, we are adapting some T2S processes to help the market operate efficiently under the tighter timetable that T+1 will bring. This includes changes to the night-time settlement process, which are planned for June 2027 ahead of the market’s migration to T+1 settlement in October 2027. We will continue working closely with market participants and other European authorities to ensure that the transition to T+1 settlement goes smoothly. Preparing for the financial system of tomorrow But while we prepare for T+1, we also need to look further ahead. Technology is reshaping finance. Distributed ledger technology and tokenisation offer opportunities not only to make today’s processes faster by enabling the near-instant transfer of securities, but potentially to simplify the architecture of finance itself. Tokenisation could bring issuance, trading, clearing, settlement, custody and asset servicing into a shared digital environment. The Eurosystem intends to be part of that transformation, and we have already moved from vision to delivery.[4] Since 30 March, the Eurosystem has been accepting marketable assets issued in central securities depositories using distributed ledger technology as eligible collateral for its credit operations.[5] We are now assessing whether, how and under what criteria DLT-based assets outside currently eligible settlement systems could become eligible collateral. We will ensure that our collateral framework keeps pace with innovation while upholding our statutory requirement for collateral to be adequate. Since 21 September, Pontes has enabled wholesale transactions in tokenised assets to be settled in central bank money. It connects market DLT platforms with our TARGET Services, bringing the safety of central bank money to the emerging world of tokenised finance.[6] To further build on this momentum, the Eurosystem will enhance the initial core functionalities of Pontes. We will do so in steps, for example by extending the operating hours significantly by mid-2027 and moving to 24/7/365 availability in 2028. We also plan to offer immediate settlement finality on the Eurosystem DLT platform as early as next year. Appia looks further ahead. It is exploring how we can build an integrated European ecosystem for tokenised finance around common standards, with central bank money continuing to provide the anchor of trust and stability. By 2028, Appia aims to deliver a blueprint setting out key findings, recommendations and principles for a safe, innovative and integrated European tokenised financial ecosystem.[7] Yesterday we published a report on the outcome of the public consultation on the Appia roadmap.[8] The consultation confirmed broad market support for developing an integrated, innovative and resilient European tokenised finance ecosystem anchored in central bank money. It also revealed a high degree of willingness among respondents to contribute actively to Appia. This provides a strong basis to develop Appia as a public-private partnership. But embracing the future does not mean discarding what already works. So, what does all this mean for T2S? Let me be very clear: T2S is not going to disappear any time soon. Different technologies and infrastructures will coexist because they are suited to different functions and different use cases. T2S will continue to serve European securities markets. At the same time, tokenised platforms will develop and new forms of financial market infrastructure will emerge. The Eurosystem’s tokenisation strategy therefore complements our continuous efforts to improve and modernise our existing TARGET Services. So we should not frame the discussion as a choice between today’s infrastructure and tomorrow’s technology. The real challenge is to enable them to coexist. We need existing and new infrastructures to work together effectively, while preserving the safety of settlement in central bank money and avoiding the emergence of new technological silos. Innovation should help Europe overcome fragmentation – it shouldn’t recreate that fragmentation in digital form. Conclusion Let me conclude. T+1, T2S, Pontes and Appia may appear to be different initiatives. But they are connected by a common purpose. We want Europe’s financial infrastructure to be robust and resilient. We want it to be efficient and innovative. And we want it to provide a foundation on which an integrated and competitive European financial market can develop. T+1 will be an important step on that journey. We now have less than a year to complete the transition. So let us keep up the momentum, intensify implementation and testing, and make Europe’s transition to T+1 a success. Thank you. I would like to thank Rémy Al Sbinati, Maria Foskolou, Gergely Kóczán, Lucia Martin Moran, Karoun Meresené and Anna Nuzzolo for their help in preparing this speech. See Lagarde, C. title: AI adoption in Europe
subtitle: Keynote speech by Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Economic Research Symposium on AI and the economy
contents: SPEECH AI adoption in Europe Keynote speech by Philip R. Lane, Member of the Executive Board of the ECB, at the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco Economic Research Symposium on AI and the economy San Francisco, 30 October 2026 My aim today is to describe how AI is reshaping the euro area economy.[1] Although the development of frontier AI models is primarily taking place in the United States and China, the adoption of AI will be a key determinant of European productivity growth in the coming years, while expenditure on AI adoption also currently constitutes a significant stimulus to the euro area economy.[2] In addition, European firms are part of the global AI supply chain, while European investors are contributing to the funding of the global buildout of AI infrastructure through equity and debt markets and the banking system. I will also describe the key patterns we see in the data, with a primary focus on how the surveys conducted by the ECB can provide insights into the AI adoption process and the implications for the financial system.[3] [4] Aggregate trends Digital investment in the euro area has expanded by 73 per cent in real terms since 2014, increasing from 2.3 per cent to 3.3 per cent of GDP (Chart 1a). While digital investment has grown far more quickly in the United States, the surge in digital investment (with an estimated clear acceleration since 2024) marks a distinct shift in the structure of the euro area economy.[5] As shown in Chart 1b, in the euro area digital investment has primarily been in intangible assets, while investment in data centres has constituted a relatively small share.[6] Chart 1 Digital investment in the euro area a) Digital investment proxy, euro area b) Digital investment proxy, euro area, with asset breakdown (2014 = 100) (EUR billion) Sources: Eurostat, ECB and ECB calculations. Notes: Chart 1a shows the digital proxy for the euro area business economy, at constant 2020 prices, indexed to 2014. The blue dots for 2025 and 2026 extend the digital investment proxy based on the annual growth of an output proxy for digital services (weighted non-seasonally adjusted production of publishing activities; computer programming, consultancy and related activities; and information service activities). Chart 1b shows a digital proxy which refers to (i) investment in non-residential buildings and structures in the information and communication sector, (ii) information and communication technology (ICT) equipment in the business economy, (iii) investment in computer software and databases (CSDBs) in the business economy, excluding the ICT sector, and (iv) total intellectual property products (IPP) investment (in CSDBs and research and development) by the ICT sector. Missing country values are estimated based on known euro area aggregates of country-sector shares. On a whole-economy basis, digital investment has increased from around 2.3 per cent of euro area GDP in 2014 to 3.0 per cent in 2024 (and looks to have increased to 3.3 per cent by the end of the first half of 2026, on the basis of updates of digital services output). The latest observations are for 2024 for euro area annual accounts and July 2026 for euro area production data. In the ECB Corporate Telephone Survey, firms report that AI has added about 10 per cent to their capital expenditure plans this year. AI-related demand has helped activity to hold up over the last two years – as reflected by the contributions of the “computers and other electronics” and “information and communication services” sectors to total market production (Chart 2a). As illustrated in Chart 2b, Purchasing Managers’ Index (PMI) indicators show that output, employment and new orders have developed considerably more favourably in the technology equipment subsector than in other manufacturing subsectors. For services, the software subsector has performed better than other services sectors in terms of output, albeit not in terms of employment and new orders. Chart 2 Effects of the global AI boom on euro area output a) Total market production b) PMIs for technology equipment and software in manufacturing and services (cumulated changes since January 2025 in per cent) (diffusion indices, average January-September 2026) Sources: Eurostat and ECB calculations Note: The latest observations are for July 2026. Sources: S&P Global and ECB calculations. Notes: Sectoral labels are taken from the July Global PMI press release. The latest observations are for September 2026. AI has been the main driver of global goods trade over the last year (Chart 3a). European firms are contributors to the global AI supply chain. Table 4 shows that AI-related exports and imports are growing quickly in the euro area, especially in relation to core data centre goods, which contain directly deployed hardware components related to AI compute, storage and networking capacity. Possibly related to differences in composition, the increase in AI import prices in the euro area is more muted than for the other major economic regions (Chart 3b). Chart 5 shows that, while AI-related price increases have contributed materially to the upward shift in goods inflation, the impact on headline inflation is limited owing to the relatively low weight of AI-exposed goods in the consumer price index (13.3 per cent in the non-energy industrial goods subcomponent and 3.4 per cent of the HICP). Notes: The figures are nominal data. Values are deviations from their respective mean over 2019-2023. “AI-related” reflects a basket of goods related to the construction and operation of AI data centres estimated by Emter et al. (2026) following Waugh (2026). The latest observations are for the second quarter of 2026. Sources: Trade Data Monitor, ECB and ECB staff calculations. Notes: Import prices are calculated as unit values. “AI goods” is a basket of goods related to AI data centre construction (Emter et al. 2026; Waugh 2026). Unless otherwise indicated, prices are in US dollars. “Asia – AI exporters” includes Hong Kong, India, Indonesia, Malaysia, Singapore, South Korea, Taiwan, Thailand and the Philippines. The latest observations are for July 2026 for the euro area, Asia and Global, August 2026 for the United States and September 2026 for China. A comparison of the AI financing plans of firms within the same country, industry and size class indicates that more tangible investment tilts financing towards external sources (Chart 23). The use of external finance for AI appears to hinge on the tangibility of the underlying investment: assets that are pledgeable or collateralisable attract external funding, whereas more intangible expenditures are financed internally. Investments in hardware and data infrastructure typically require large upfront capital outlays that exceed available internal cash flow while providing pledgeable collateral, prompting firms to seek complementary external funding. In contrast, employee training represents a smaller, more incremental and intangible expense that firms can more readily finance out of retained earnings. Overall, the findings highlight the importance of collateral in securing external financing. This pattern may also point to a potential financing gap for intangible investments, which are critical for building long-term AI capabilities. Turning to bond pricing, Chart 25a (left panel) shows that AI-exposed non-financial firms in the STOXX Europe 600 exhibit lower option-adjusted spreads than their non-exposed counterparts, although this pattern has reversed somewhat recently. In particular, both the median and interquartile range of spreads for AI-exposed firms have shifted downward in most years of the sample period. Concurrently, these firms have issued a larger share of bonds with maturities exceeding ten years, whereas non-exposed issuers exhibit a greater concentration of bonds at intermediate maturities. Checking for credit risk (Expected Default Frequency, leverage, profitability and size), bond characteristics and bond fixed effects, AI exposure is estimated to correspond to around 5 basis points tighter spreads (Chart 25a, right panel). This combination of lower spreads and longer maturities suggests more favourable debt financing conditions for AI-exposed firms, since longer maturities would typically be associated with higher spreads in the absence of such advantages. Taken together, these results indicate a modest but robust relation between AI exposure and a lower market-implied cost of debt financing. In relation to the equity market, AI-exposed firms recorded higher median annual stock returns than non-exposed firms in most years of the sample (Chart 25b, left panel). AI-exposed firms also tend to trade at higher price-earnings ratios, consistent with investors assigning higher valuations to their expected future earnings and, potentially, with a longer-duration equity profile. AI firms in general also tend to be more liquid than their non-AI peers (Chart 30). Conclusions This speech has highlighted that AI is currently a significant contributor to growth in the euro area, driven by both expenditure on AI adoption and the role of European firms in the global AI supply chain. Surveys of firms and households indicate significant AI adoption rates, albeit unevenly distributed across sectors and demographic groups. A striking pattern is that European households are net positive about the employment impact of AI. However, the AI adoption process is still at a relatively early stage and the extent and timing of the economy-wide transformative potential of AI remain highly uncertain. The European financial system has responded to the external financing needs generated by increased AI activity, even if internal funding remains the most important source of funding. European investors are also major investors in foreign AI equities and the euro-denominated bond issuances by American hyperscalers, even if the latter are primarily funded by a lower allocation to US Treasury bonds. Looking ahead, tracking the near-term and medium-term implications of AI will remain high on the analytical agenda at the ECB.
